I am 66 years old, and I have been working this land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. I never went to school, but the land has been my teacher for over forty years. I have about 8 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and I know every corner of it.

This year, like every year, I will plant **winter wheat** and **summer maize** in rotation. That is the way of our village. Wheat goes into the ground around the tenth month, sleeps through the winter under the snow, and comes up green in the spring. We harvest it in early June, and the very same day or the next, we put in the maize. By the time the autumn winds come, the maize is dry and ready for the cob picker. I do not know any other system that fits our land and our climate so well.

For the **winter wheat**, I will till the soil with the rotary tiller after the maize stubble is dealt with. I will sow about 15 kilograms of improved wheat seed per mu — I usually save some seed from the previous year and buy a little from the supply shop in town to make sure it is clean and strong. I will spread compound fertilizer as a basal dressing, about 50 kg per mu, and top-dress with urea when the wheat joints in the spring. I will irrigate three times: once before winter to help it survive the cold, once at green-up, and once at grain-filling. I will spray pesticides four times — herbicide first, then fungicide and insecticide as needed when the weather turns damp.

For the **summer maize**, I will not till the land. I learned this from my neighbors and from the agricultural extension people — we sow the maize directly into the wheat stubble, which saves fuel, time, and keeps the moisture in the ground. I will buy one and a half packages of hybrid maize seed per mu from the seed shop. Hybrid seed costs money, but the yield is much better than the old varieties, and everyone in our county uses it. I will irrigate twice, once right after sowing if the soil is dry, and once at the big喇叭口 stage. I will spray pesticides three times to control weeds and the corn borer.

I do not try fancy crops like vegetables or cotton — I am too old to learn new tricks, and the wheat-maize rotation gives me steady grain and straw for my household. The prices are not what they used to be, but with the government grain subsidy and my own labor, I can get by.
